children: By Anita Hamilton and Al Root
The Federal Aviation Administration on Tuesday formally certified Boeing's 737 MAX 10 to fly.
It's good news. So why isn't the stock up?
The MAX 10 is the longest version of the MAX, with more than 1,500 orders from 30 customers. Deliveries will start in the coming months, according to the company.
Approval is a positive. Still, Boeing stock was mostly flat in after-hours trading. That's a small surprise. MAX Certification was supposed to be a catalyst to send shares higher.

Boeing stock could use a catalyst. Through Tuesday trading, shares were down 12% year to date after falling 16% since the start of the Iran War. Higher fuel prices have sapped investor enthusiasm for aerospace stocks.
Boeing has also had some hiccups. It's had trouble expanding MAX production, and a software glitch was discovered that can impact MAX landings. The FAA said the glitch wasn't a safety issue.

The stock might not go up immediately, but Boeing needs the MAX 10 to reach its goals of higher deliveries and free cash flow. Wall Street projects 2028 deliveries of 830 jets and free cash flow of almost $10 billion.
Boeing is on pace to deliver about 670 jets in 2026, up from 600 in 2025.
The approval comes after years of delays. Next up is the approval for the 777X wide-body jet. Certification of that jet also depends on some engine work by GE Aerospace.

"Certification activity is likely pushed into 2027, with Boeing still expecting initial deliveries then," wrote Jefferies analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu in a Tuesday report. "The 777-9 has 542 orders as of September end, representing 81% of the 777X backlog."
